title: Finding Elements
jobContext: Your boss needs to update the headline on the company website every morning. Instead of editing HTML by hand, they ask you to write a script that finds the headline element and changes the text. First step: find it.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn
By the end of this lesson, you'll write a function that finds an element on a webpage and reads the text inside it. We'll explain every single piece — even things that seem obvious.
What Is a Webpage Made Of?

A webpage is like a tree of boxes (elements). Each box has a tag name like
or

. Some boxes have an id — a unique name tag. For example:
Welcome to CodeLabs
has the id "main-heading" and the text "Welcome to CodeLabs" inside.
The `document` Object

JavaScript has a built-in variable called **document**. Think of it as a remote control for the entire webpage. If you want to find, read, or change anything on the page, you use document. You don't need to create it — it's always there.

// document is already there, ready to use
document; // This is the whole webpage
Finding an Element with `getElementById`

To find a specific element on the page, use the method **getElementById**. A **method** is just a tool attached to something — here, it's a tool attached to document. You write: document.getElementById('main-heading'). The 'main-heading' is the id of the element you want to find.
Saving Things in Variables with `let`
A **variable** is like a labeled box where you store something so you can use it later. You create a box with the keyword **let**, give it a name, and put a value inside with =.
You can name variables almost anything. Good names describe what's inside: element, heading, btn, output. Avoid single letters like x or y.
Reading Text with `textContent`

Every element has a property called **textContent**. A **property** is a piece of information attached to an element. textContent gives you the text inside that element — nothing else, no HTML tags, just the words.
What Is a Function?

A **function** is a reusable block of code with a name. Think of it like a recipe: you write the steps once, then you can run them anytime by saying the recipe's name. You create one with the **function** keyword.
What Is `return`?

The **return** statement sends a value back to whoever called your function. If a function is like a vending machine, return is the slot where your snack comes out. Without return, the function runs but gives nothing back.
Every function call turns into whatever value you return. getFive() turns into the number 5 wherever you use it.
Putting It All Together

Your task: write a function called getHeadingText that finds the element with id 'main-heading' and returns its text. Inside the function, you will: (1) find the element with document.getElementById, (2) save it in a variable, (3) return the variable's textContent.

hints: Use document.getElementById('main-heading') to find the element
Save the element in a variable: let el = document.getElementById(...)
Return el.textContent — that gives you the text inside

title: Click & Respond
jobContext: Your team is building an app and needs a button that does something when clicked. Not just looking pretty — when a user taps it, the page should update. Your job: wire up the button so clicking it shows a message.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn
You'll learn how to make a button react when someone clicks it. We'll explain what addEventListener does, what a callback function is, and what that strange () => arrow means.
Review: Finding Elements
From lesson 1: use document.getElementById('some-id') to find an element on the page. You'll need this to find the button and the output area.
What Is an Event?

An **event** is something that happens on the page — a click, a key press, a mouse move, a form submit. The browser watches for these and can run code when they happen. The most common event is 'click'.
What Is `addEventListener`?
**addEventListener** is a method that tells an element: "When this event happens, run this code." You give it two things: the event name (like 'click') and the code to run (a function).
What Is a Callback Function?

A **callback function** is a function you give to something to call later. Like giving a friend your phone number: they'll call you when they're ready. Here, you give addEventListener a function, and it calls that function when the click happens.
What Is an Arrow Function `() =>`?

An **arrow function** is a shorter way to write a function. Instead of function name() { }, you write () => { }. The () is where inputs would go, the => (arrow) means "goes to", and the { } contain the steps. It's faster to type and very common in modern JavaScript.
Don't let () => scare you. Read it as: "when this happens, do this." The () is empty because the click event doesn't need extra input. If it needed input, the name would go inside ().
Review: Setting `textContent`
You can change what text an element shows by assigning to its textContent property with =. This replaces whatever text was there before.
Putting It All Together
Your task: write a function setupButton that finds the button with id 'action-btn' and the output element with id 'output'. Then tell the button: "when clicked, set output's text to 'Clicked!'".
Notice setupButton doesn't return anything — it just sets things up. The actual work happens later when someone clicks the button.

hints: Find the button: let btn = document.getElementById('action-btn')
Find the output: let output = document.getElementById('output')

title: Change the Page
jobContext: Your app needs to show a list of cards — like a news feed or a product catalog. But the cards don't exist in the HTML yet. You need to write code that builds each card from scratch and adds it to the page. Today: build the card factory.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn
You'll learn how to create brand-new HTML elements in JavaScript, put content inside them, add CSS classes, and return the finished element. This is how apps build things on the fly.
Creating Elements with `document.createElement`

**document.createElement('tag')** creates a new HTML element in memory. It doesn't appear on the page yet — it's like blowing up a balloon but not letting go. You give it the tag name as a string: 'div', 'h3', 'p', etc.
Adding CSS Classes with `classList.add`
**classList** is a property that holds all the CSS classes on an element. **classList.add('card')** adds the class 'card' to the element. This lets you style your new element with existing CSS rules.
What Are Function Parameters?

**Parameters** are inputs that a function receives. They go inside the parentheses in the function definition. Think of them as settings that change what the function does. When someone calls createCard('Hello', 'World'), the value 'Hello' goes into the title parameter and 'World' goes into body.
Review: Setting `textContent`
Remember from lesson 1: you can read textContent to get the text, and you can set it with = to put text inside an element.
Nesting Elements with `appendChild`
**appendChild** puts one element inside another as a child. You call it on the parent element and pass the child element. The child becomes the last thing inside the parent.
You can appendChild as many times as you want. Each call adds one more child to the end. Order matters — the first thing you append appears first.
Review: Returning a Value
The function needs to give back the card element it built. Use **return** to send the card back to whoever called the function.
Putting It All Together
Your task: write createCard(title, body) that creates a div with class 'card', puts an h3 with title and a p with body inside it, and returns the finished card.
The order of your code matters. You must create an element before you can add content to it. You must add content before you append it. And you must append children before returning the parent.

hints: Create h3 with: let heading = document.createElement('h3') and set heading.textContent = title
Create p with: let para = document.createElement('p') and set para.textContent = body
